items.prompt: Which built-in function returns the number of items in a list?

options.label: count()
length()
len()
size()

items.explanation: `len()` is the built-in for the number of items in a sequence.

items.prompt: Which symbol starts a single-line comment in Python?
Sam is writing a script that asks a user for their name. He needs a built-in function that shows a message and reads a line of text typed by the user. Which function should he use?

options.label: read()
input()
get()
scan()

items.explanation: `input()` prompts the user and returns the typed text as a string.

items.prompt: Which of these statements about Python strings are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: They can be written with single or double quotes
They can be indexed starting at 0
They are immutable once created
Individual characters can be reassigned with `s[0] = 'x'`

items.explanation: Strings accept either quote style, are immutable, and are zero-indexed.

items.prompt: What does `5 // 2` evaluate to in Python 3?

options.label: 2.5, because `//` divides normally
2, because `//` divides and rounds down
1, because `//` gives the remainder
3, because `//` rounds up

items.prompt: Why does `t = (1, 2, 3)` followed by `t[0] = 9` raise a `TypeError`?

options.label: Tuple indexes start at 1, so index 0 is not a valid position
Tuples are immutable, so their items cannot be reassigned
Integers in a tuple are constants, though strings in one could change
Tuples allow assignment only to their last element, not the first

items.explanation: Tuples are immutable, so item assignment is unsupported.

items.prompt: You are counting word frequencies into an initially empty dict `counts`. Which loop body correctly handles a word `w` seen for the first time?

options.label: `counts[w] = counts[w] + 1`
`counts[w] += 1`
`counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1`
`counts.update({w: counts[w] + 1})`

items.explanation: `get(w, 0)` supplies a default so unseen words start at 0.

`print(f(2))`

items.prompt: `counter = 0`, then `def inc(): counter += 1`, and calling `inc()` raises `UnboundLocalError`. What is the cause?

options.label: Functions can't read module-level names unless they are passed in as arguments or declared nonlocal
`counter` is read before `inc` is defined, so the name does not exist yet when the call runs
Integers are immutable, so `+=` can never rebind a module-level name from inside a function
The assignment in `+=` makes `counter` local, and it is read before being set

items.explanation: Any assignment in a function body makes the name local for the whole function, so the read in `+=` fails.

items.prompt: Given `class Cart: items = []` and `def add(self, x): self.items.append(x)`, two separate Cart objects show each other's items. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: Each instance receives its own copy of `items` the first time it is created
Declaring `items` as a tuple would still allow `append` to work on it
Setting `self.items = []` inside `__init__` would give each instance its own list
Writing `self.items = self.items + [x]` would create an instance attribute and stop the sharing
`append` mutates the single list stored on the class, so both instances see the change

items.explanation: The list lives on the class; mutation is shared, while assignment through self creates per-instance attributes.

items.prompt: A loop registers callbacks: `for name in names: handlers.append(lambda: print(name))`. After the loop, every handler prints the last name. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: Each lambda stores the value of `name` at creation, but the loop reuses one string object and mutates it in place each pass
Each lambda copies `name` when created, but `print` later overwrites the copies when the handlers are called in order
Appending to a list rebinds earlier stored functions to the newest lambda, so all list entries become the same function
The closure looks up `name` when it is called, and by then the shared variable holds the last value

items.explanation: Closures capture variables, not values, so lookup happens at call time (late binding).

items.prompt: You store 1 million immutable (x, y) points and use them as dict keys. Criteria: hashable by value, modest memory, readable field names. Which representation is best?

options.label: A plain `@dataclass`, which has named fields and a generated `__eq__` and `__hash__`, so equal instances work as dict keys
`typing.NamedTuple`, which is immutable, hashes by value, is compact, and has named fields
A plain class with `__slots__`, since slots save memory and the default `__hash__` uses the field values
A dict like `{'x': 1, 'y': 2}` per point, since named keys are clear and dicts hash by their contents

items.explanation: NamedTuple is a tuple subclass: hashable by value, compact, with named access.

items.prompt: A library function parses a port number from config text. Criteria: callers must be able to catch a library-specific error, and the original cause must remain visible in the traceback. Which handler is best?

options.label: `except ValueError as e: print(e); sys.exit(1)`
`except ValueError as e: raise ConfigError(f"bad port: {e}") from None`
`except ValueError as e: raise ConfigError("bad port") from e`
`except ValueError as e: log.error(e); return 80  # default port`

items.explanation: Raising a custom exception `from e` gives a catchable type and preserves the cause chain.

items.prompt: Profiling shows 5 million small `Point` objects with fixed attributes `x` and `y` dominate memory use. Which judgement about adding `__slots__ = ('x', 'y')` is best supported?

options.label: It stores attributes in a compact C-level layout, so it saves memory only when the module is also compiled with Cython.
It makes attribute reads faster and the instances thread-safe, because slot storage is updated atomically without any locking.
It removes the per-instance `__dict__` to save memory, but blocks undeclared attributes and complicates multiple inheritance.
It changes how attributes are documented and type-checked, but instance memory stays the same unless the class is also made frozen.

items.explanation: Slots drop the per-instance dict, saving memory at the cost of flexibility.

items.prompt: Design a helper that runs `grep` on a user-supplied filename. Constraints: no shell injection through the filename, a nonzero exit must raise, and stdout must come back as `str`. Which elements belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Call `os.system(cmd)` and treat its return value as the text printed by the command.
Pass `check=True` so a nonzero exit status raises `CalledProcessError`.
Build one command string with an f-string and pass `shell=True`, wrapping the filename in single quotes.
Pass `capture_output=True, text=True` so stdout is returned as a `str`.
Pass the command as a list like `["grep", "-n", pattern, path]` with the default `shell=False`.

items.explanation: List arguments avoid the shell, `check=True` raises on failure, and `capture_output` with `text` returns a string.

items.prompt: Design a context manager `timed` that times a block. Constraints: it must record elapsed time even if the block raises, and it must not hide the exception. Which `__exit__` design meets both?

options.label: Record the time only when `exc_type` is `None`, and return `False` in every other case
Record the time, then `return True` so the block's code can finish cleanly after the error
Record the time, then return `None` so any exception from the block keeps propagating
Record the time in `__enter__` only, because `__exit__` is skipped when the block raises

items.explanation: `__exit__` always runs; returning a falsy value lets the exception propagate.

items.prompt: Design `collect(item, bucket=...)` that appends `item` and returns the list. Constraints: a call without `bucket` gets a fresh list each time, and a caller-passed empty list must be the very list that gets mutated. Which design meets both?

options.label: `bucket=None`, then `bucket = bucket or []` at the start
`bucket=[]`, then `bucket.clear()` at the start
`bucket=None`, then `if bucket is None: bucket = []`
`bucket=[]`, then `bucket = list(bucket)` at the start

items.explanation: An `is None` check creates a fresh list only when none was passed and keeps the caller's list.
